claims.text: The FeCoNiCrP baseline alloy is prone to modest glass-forming ability and low thermal stability in its amorphous state.
Adding approximately 2 at% Nb to FeCoNiCrP will improve its glass-forming ability.
Adding approximately 2 at% Nb to FeCoNiCrP will improve the thermal stability of its amorphous state.
The proposed intervention is to add approximately 2 at% Nb to the alloy melt.
Nb is a large-atomic-radius transition metal relative to the base-alloy elements.
The beneficial effect requires Nb to remain uniformly distributed without forming Nb-rich segregated phases.
Rapid solidification by melt spinning at a cooling rate near 10^3 K/s is an appropriate processing condition for testing the intervention.
Keeping the Nb concentration below approximately 3 at% will ensure that Nb remains a dilute solute.
Nb addition increases atomic-size mismatch and local atomic-packing disorder.
The presence of Nb disrupts local crystallographic order.
The larger atomic radius of Nb introduces local lattice or packing distortions.
Nb-induced local distortions increase the activation barrier for crystal nucleation during cooling.
Disruption of local order impedes diffusion during subsequent thermal annealing.
Increased nucleation barriers promote glass formation.
Impeded diffusion raises the crystallization-onset temperature.
Relative to identically processed Nb-free FeCoNiCrP, the Nb-added alloy will have a lower critical cooling rate for glass formation.
Relative to identically processed Nb-free FeCoNiCrP, the Nb-added alloy will have a crystallization-onset temperature approximately 20–30 K higher, assuming uniform Nb distribution.
Nb segregation or concentrations above approximately 3 at% may cause phase separation and negate the improvements.

contradictions.description: Uniform Nb distribution is stated as a precondition for the hypothesized benefit, and segregation is identified as an out-of-boundary case that may negate the effect; nevertheless, observing segregation is also declared to falsify the hypothesis. Failure to satisfy a stated applicability condition does not by itself test the conditional claim.

The hypothesis predicts two improvements, but the falsification rule requires both the 20–30 K shift and the critical-cooling-rate reduction to be absent. A result in which only one predicted improvement fails is not classified, despite contradicting part of the conjunctive prediction.
